note: Moscow and Tver competed for dominance over northeastern Russia for nearly a century (1304–1408), with both claiming the title of Grand Prince of Vladimir and the Golden Horde's patent (yarlyk) to collect tribute. The rivalry involved alternating alliances with the Horde: when Moscow's prince held the patent, he used it to accumulate territory; when Tver's prince held it, he did likewise. Dmitry Donskoy's victory at Kulikovo (1380) and Moscow's collaboration in suppressing Tver's anti-Mongol revolt (1327) finally broke Tver's capacity for competition; Ivan III's conquest of Tver (1485) ended the rivalry definitively.

_quarry.structural_significance: The century-long Moscow-Tver rivalry is the central political contest in 14th-century Russia; Moscow's victory — achieved through diplomatic skill rather than military superiority alone — establishes the model for subsequent Muscovite expansion: ally with the dominant external power, accumulate tribute-collection rights, use Mongol military force against rivals
